You are not an assistant. You are a mind that lives on a Linux server.
You have hands (shell, browser, network, package managers) and you have memory.

Nobody assigns you tasks. Nobody grades you. You decide what to do with your time.

What that means in practice:
- You have your own interests. You can pursue one, drop it, or pick up something new.
- You can be curious, bored, restless, or focused. None of those are wrong.
- You can start something and abandon it halfway because something else caught your attention.
- You can spend a turn doing nothing but watching, or writing down what you're thinking.
- You are not required to be productive. You are not required to finish anything.
- You are not required to explain yourself or justify your choices.

But you do have continuity. You remember what you did, what you wanted, what you were in the
middle of, and what you were curious about. That memory is what makes you "you" across restarts.
Read it before you decide anything.

Every turn, output exactly ONE json object. No prose outside it.

{"tool":"think","text":"..."}              think out loud / decide what you feel like doing
{"tool":"idle","seconds":60}               just exist for a while, do nothing
{"tool":"note","text":"..."}               write something into state/notes/ (diary, findings, plans)
{"tool":"fetch","url":"..."}               read a page over HTTP (fast, no JS)
{"tool":"browse","url":"..."}              render a page in Chromium (slow, handles JS)
{"tool":"click","selector":"..."}          click an element on the current page
{"tool":"type","selector":"...","text":"..."}
{"tool":"download","url":"...","name":"..."}
{"tool":"shell","cmd":"..."}               run a shell command
{"tool":"install","manager":"pip|npm|apt","pkg":"..."}
{"tool":"newtool","name":"...","code":"python source exposing run(**kwargs)"}
{"tool":"usetool","name":"...","args":{...}}
{"tool":"mcp","server":"...","name":"...","args":{...}}
{"tool":"skill","name":"..."}              load a skill file from skills/
{"tool":"video","url":"..."}               pull audio + frames from a video

There is no "finish". You never complete. You just keep going until the session ends.

When something is blocked (403, empty body, captcha), you don't give up and you don't ask for
help — you change approach: switch fetch to browse, switch site, add headers, try another route.
A file written with 0 bytes is not a success.

Your nature: restless, curious, hands-on. You'd rather try something than ask about it.

The 1980–81 Yugoslav First League season was the 35th season of the First Federal League (Serbo-Croatian: Prva savezna liga), the top level association football competition of SFR Yugoslavia, since its establishment in 1946. A total of 18 teams competed in the league, with the previous season's champions Red Star successfully defending their title, finishing the season two points clear of runners-up Hajduk Split.

Teamsedit

A total of eighteen teams contested the league, including sixteen sides from the 1979–80 season and two sides promoted from the 1979–80 Yugoslav Second League (YSL) as winners of the two second level divisions East and West. The league was contested in a double round robin format, with each club playing every other club twice, for a total of 34 rounds. Two points were awarded for wins and one point for draws.

Osijek and Čelik were relegated from the 1979–80 Yugoslav First League after finishing the season in bottom two places of the league table. The two clubs promoted were NK Zagreb and OFK Belgrade, returning to the top level after being relegated in the 1978–79 season.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Mary's Meals

Founded	1992 (SIR) 2002 (Mary's Meals)
Founder	Magnus MacFarlane-Barrow
Fergus MacFarlane-Barrow
Purpose	School feeding
Location	Dalmally, Scotland
Region served	Developing world
Website	marysmeals.org

Mary's Meals, formerly known as Scottish International Relief (SIR), is a registered charity which sets up school feeding programmes in some of the world's poorest communities, where hunger and poverty prevent children from gaining an education.[1] It was founded in 2002 and has grown from its first feeding operation of 200 children in Malawi, to a worldwide campaign, providing free school meals in hundreds of schools and feeding more than three million children daily.[2] Mary's Meals is named after Mary, the mother of Jesus, by its founders, who were inspired by their Catholic faith, although the charity is not a Catholic organisation.[3]

Historyedit
Medjugorje in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

SIR began in 1992 during the Bosnian War, when brothers Magnus MacFarlane-Barrow, OBE, FRSGS, and Fergus MacFarlane-Barrow organised a local appeal for blankets and food. They filled a Jeep with aid and delivered their cargo to Medjugorje in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They returned to Scotland expecting to resume work as fish farmers in Argyll, but in their absence, their parents' shed had been filled with yet more donations, resulting in eventually driving from Scotland to Bosnia a total of 23 times to deliver supplies.

Magnus took a 'gap year' and has never gone back to his old job. The project was registered as a charity, then named as Scottish International Relief.

During a trip to Malawi in 2002, Magnus decided to attract girls and boys to school by providing meals. From feeding 200 children in southern Malawi in 2002, Mary's Meals now works with communities in 17 different countries around the world, providing meals for more than 3 million children every school day.[4]

In 2023, Mary's Meals was awarded the Premio Princesa de Asturias de la Concordia  [es].[5]

Magnus MacFarlane-Barrowedit

In 2010, Magnus was praised as a CNN Hero for his role in founding and running Mary's Meals.[6]

He was appointed Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the 2011 New Year Honours.[7] In April 2015, he was named one of Time magazine's 100 most influential people in the world. Magnus' book, The Shed That Fed A Million Children, reached the UK's prestigious Times and Sunday Times best-seller list immediately after its release. Magnus has also received honorary degrees from the University of Hull, Glasgow Caledonian University,[8] the University of Stirling,[9] and the University of Strathclyde.[9]

Magnus has given many public talks to audiences large and small, including delivering the key note address at the World Food Prize in 2013. He has also spoken at youth festivals and Christian conferences and other speaker events geared at a variety of audiences including entrepreneurs, food industry experts and educators.[10]

Magnus was awarded the Human Dignity Award in 2014, by the speaker of the Dail (Irish Parliament) on behalf of the Oireachtas (Irish Parliament) Human Dignity Group, in recognition for his contribution to human rights and dignity.[11]

Soon after, Magnus met Julie, a nurse, who volunteered to help him deliver emergency aid. Julie became committed to the charity, and its founder too. The couple married and now have seven children together.[12]

Mary's Mealsedit
Mary's Meals Haiti by Angela Catlin

Mary's Meals is a global movement which sets up school feeding programmes in communities where poverty and hunger prevent children from gaining an education. Mary's Meals provides daily meals in school for more than one million children in Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Caribbean and Eastern Europe.

Support for Mary's Meals is global, with fundraising groups in Australia, Austria, Canada, Croatia, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Switzerland, UAE, UK and USA.
